title: Convolutional networks: Neocognitron, LeNet
text:
CHAPTER 13. BACKPROPAGATION AND CONNECTIONISM
SECTION 13.3. CONVOLUTIONAL NETWORKS: FROM THE NEOCOGNITRON TO LENET

A fully connected network treats an image as an unstructured list of numbers. It does not know that neighboring pixels are related, or that a "7" in the corner is the same as a "7" in the center. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) build these facts into the architecture: units look at small local regions, and the same feature detector is applied everywhere in the image. The idea came from neuroscience (Hubel and Wiesel), was turned into a hierarchical model by Kunihiko Fukushima (the Neocognitron), and became a practical, backpropagation-trained technology with Yann LeCun's LeNet at Bell Labs, which read zip codes and bank checks in the 1990s. CNNs then powered the deep learning breakthrough of 2012 (Chapter 16). This section covers the history and the arithmetic, which every engineer working with cameras should know.

1. Hubel and Wiesel: the visual cortex

David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel, working first at Johns Hopkins and then Harvard, recorded the activity of individual neurons in the visual cortex of cats (and later monkeys) while showing them simple patterns. Their paper "Receptive fields of single neurones in the cat's striate cortex" appeared in 1959 in the Journal of Physiology, followed by more detailed work in the early 1960s. They found:

  - Each neuron responds only to stimuli in a small region of the visual field, its receptive field.
  - "Simple cells" respond to bars or edges at a particular orientation and position.
  - "Complex cells" respond to an oriented bar anywhere within a somewhat larger region: they are tolerant to small shifts of position.
  - Neurons are organized in columns by orientation preference and by eye dominance, and nearby neurons represent nearby parts of the visual field.

Hubel and Wiesel shared the 1981 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (with Roger Sperry) for these discoveries. The idea of a hierarchy, with simple local feature detectors whose outputs are pooled by cells with some position tolerance, and repeated at higher levels, became the blueprint for CNNs.

2. Fukushima's Neocognitron (1979-1980)

Kunihiko Fukushima, a researcher at NHK's (the Japanese broadcaster's) science and technical research laboratories, built neural network models of vision. After an earlier model called the Cognitron (1975), he introduced the Neocognitron in 1979 in Japanese and in English in 1980 ("Neocognitron: A Self-organizing Neural Network Model for a Mechanism of Pattern Recognition Unaffected by Shift in Position," Biological Cybernetics). It had:

  - S-cells (after simple cells): each detects a feature in a small local region; all S-cells in a "plane" share the same weights, so the same feature is detected at every position. This is weight sharing, the essence of convolution.
  - C-cells (after complex cells): each combines the outputs of nearby S-cells detecting the same feature, so the response tolerates small shifts. This is pooling.
  - Several alternating S and C layers, so features become more complex and more position-tolerant at higher levels, until the top layer responds to whole patterns (for example, digits) regardless of position.

The Neocognitron's weights were learned mainly by unsupervised, competitive "self-organization" (and in some versions with supervision layer by layer), not by end-to-end backpropagation. It recognized handwritten characters with tolerance to shift and distortion. In architecture, it was a deep convolutional network a decade before LeNet. Fukushima also used a rectifying activation (outputs that are zero for negative input and linear for positive), an early form of the ReLU used in modern networks.

3. Convolution arithmetic

A 2D convolutional layer applies a small kernel (filter) K of size k x k to every position of the input. For a single-channel input X and output Y (technically cross-correlation, but universally called convolution in deep learning):

    Y[i][j] = b + sum_(u=0..k-1) sum_(v=0..k-1) K[u][v] * X[i+u][j+v]

With C_in input channels and C_out output channels, each output channel has its own kernel for each input channel:

    Y[c][i][j] = b[c] + sum_(c'=1..C_in) sum_u sum_v K[c][c'][u][v] * X[c'][i+u][j+v]

Output size. For input size n, kernel k, padding p (zeros added on each side) and stride s:

    n_out = floor((n + 2p - k) / s) + 1

Examples: 32 input, 5x5 kernel, no padding, stride 1: 28. With p = 2: 32 ("same" padding). Stride 2 halves the size.

Parameters versus connections. A convolutional layer with C_in = 3, C_out = 64, k = 3 has 64 * 3 * 3 * 3 + 64 = 1,792 parameters regardless of image size. A fully connected layer mapping a 224 x 224 x 3 image (150,528 values) to just 64 units would need about 9.6 million weights. Weight sharing cuts the number of parameters enormously and encodes the prior that the same feature can appear anywhere.

Translation equivariance: shifting the input shifts the output feature maps the same way. Pooling then adds partial invariance.

Pooling. Max pooling over 2 x 2 regions with stride 2 keeps the largest value of each block, reducing each spatial dimension by half (discarding 75 percent of the activations). Average pooling (subsampling) takes the mean; LeNet used trainable subsampling (average times a coefficient plus a bias).

Receptive field. Stacking layers enlarges the region of the input each unit sees. Two 3 x 3 convolutions give a 5 x 5 receptive field; three give 7 x 7; pooling multiplies the growth. Deep layers see large parts of the image, so local operations compose into global recognition, the answer to the "global properties" concern of Minsky and Papert (Section 10.3).

Connection to signal processing. For a mechatronics engineer, a convolutional layer is a bank of 2D FIR filters, like the Sobel edge detector

    Gx = [[-1, 0, 1],
          [-2, 0, 2],
          [-1, 0, 1]]

except that the coefficients are learned. Trained CNNs' first layers typically learn oriented edge and color-blob detectors, resembling Gabor filters and Hubel and Wiesel's simple cells.

4. LeCun at Bell Labs: backpropagation plus convolution

Yann LeCun, after his PhD in Paris (where he had developed a form of backpropagation) and a postdoc with Hinton in Toronto, joined AT&T Bell Laboratories in 1988. His group combined convolution, weight sharing and end-to-end training by backpropagation: the gradient of the loss with respect to a shared kernel weight is simply the sum of the gradients at all positions where it is used.

The 1989 work. LeCun and colleagues trained a CNN to recognize handwritten zip code digits provided by the US Postal Service (papers in 1989, including "Backpropagation Applied to Handwritten Zip Code Recognition" in Neural Computation). Inputs were 16 x 16 grayscale digit images. The network learned its convolution kernels directly from images. On the postal data it reached an error rate of about 1 percent (with some rejection of uncertain cases, as reported in the papers). Other groups in the late 1980s also trained convolutional or shift-invariant networks by backpropagation, including Alexander Waibel's time-delay neural network (TDNN, 1987-1989) for speech, which applied shared weights over time, and Wei Zhang and colleagues (1988) for character recognition.

LeNet-5 (1998). The best-known version was described by LeCun, Léon Bottou, Yoshua Bengio and Patrick Haffner in "Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition," Proceedings of the IEEE, volume 86, November 1998. Its layers (input 32 x 32):

    C1: convolution, 6 maps of 28 x 28, 5x5 kernels
    S2: subsampling, 6 maps of 14 x 14
    C3: convolution, 16 maps of 10 x 10, 5x5 kernels
        (each map connected to a subset of S2 maps)
    S4: subsampling, 16 maps of 5 x 5
    C5: convolution, 120 maps of 1 x 1 (5x5 kernels over the 5x5 maps)
    F6: fully connected, 84 units
    Output: 10 units (one per digit)

The sizes follow the formula: 32 - 5 + 1 = 28; 28 / 2 = 14; 14 - 5 + 1 = 10; 10 / 2 = 5; 5 - 5 + 1 = 1. The network had about 60,000 trainable parameters. The paper also introduced graph transformer networks for recognizing whole strings of characters, trained globally.

MNIST. The paper's benchmark was MNIST (Modified NIST), built by LeCun, Corinna Cortes and Christopher Burges from US National Institute of Standards and Technology handwriting databases: 60,000 training and 10,000 test images of 28 x 28 grayscale digits, written by Census Bureau employees and high school students. For two decades MNIST was the "hello world" of machine learning. LeNet-5 achieved test error below 1 percent; later methods reached about 0.2 percent and below.

Training cost. On the hardware of the 1990s, training a LeNet took days or weeks of CPU time; Wikipedia's account of one version reports about two weeks on a SPARCstation 10. The same network trains in seconds to minutes on a modern GPU.

5. Deployment: reading checks

LeNet-based systems were among the first neural networks deployed at scale. AT&T and NCR developed check-reading systems. A LeNet ran on a DSP chip (the AT&T DSP-32C) in ATMs that read the numerical amounts on deposited checks. NCR deployed a similar system in large check-reading machines in bank back offices from June 1996, and by 2001 it was estimated to read about 20 million checks a day, around 10 percent of all checks in the United States, according to commonly cited figures. Neural networks were thus doing real, money-handling work in the late 1990s, during the period when the field was out of fashion.

6. Why CNNs worked, and why they paused

Why it worked:

  - Strong, correct priors: locality and translation equivariance match images.
  - Far fewer parameters than fully connected networks, so less overfitting on the small datasets of the time.
  - End-to-end training: features were learned for the task instead of hand-designed.

Why they did not take over computer vision in the 1990s and 2000s:

  - Compute: larger images and more classes needed far more computation than CPUs provided.
  - Data: there were no labeled datasets of millions of natural images until ImageNet (2009).
  - Competition: hand-designed features (SIFT, 1999; HOG, 2005) with support vector machines or boosting dominated object recognition and detection benchmarks; the Viola-Jones face detector (2001) used boosted simple features and ran in real time on cameras.
  - Training deep networks was still considered difficult.

In 2012, AlexNet, a much larger CNN trained on ImageNet with two GPUs and using ReLU and dropout (Chapter 16), cut the error rate dramatically on the ImageNet challenge. Architecturally it was LeNet's direct descendant. VGG, GoogLeNet, ResNet and the CNN backbones in modern robots, phones, cars and factory inspection systems followed. Vision transformers (2020) later challenged CNNs, but convolution remains widely used, particularly on embedded hardware.

7. CNNs in mechatronics

Today CNNs are standard in:

  - Machine vision for inspection (detecting surface defects, reading labels and codes).
  - Object detection and pose estimation for robotic picking (detectors in the YOLO family and others).
  - Semantic segmentation for mobile robots and autonomous vehicles.
  - 1D CNNs on time series: vibration signals for bearing fault detection, motor current signatures, audio. A 1D convolution over a sensor signal is an FIR filter bank whose taps are learned.
  - Embedded inference on microcontrollers and edge accelerators, with quantized (8-bit integer) weights; small CNNs comparable in size to LeNet run on Cortex-M class microcontrollers.

8. Summary

  - Hubel and Wiesel (1959 onward; Nobel 1981) found local receptive fields, simple and complex cells, and a hierarchy in visual cortex.
  - Fukushima's Neocognitron (1979-1980) implemented a hierarchy of weight-sharing S-cells (convolution) and pooling C-cells, trained mainly by self-organization.
  - Convolution: Y = b + sum K * X over a local window; output size floor((n + 2p - k)/s) + 1; weight sharing gives translation equivariance and few parameters; pooling adds tolerance; stacking grows the receptive field.
  - LeCun's group at Bell Labs trained CNNs end-to-end by backpropagation: zip codes (1989, about 1 percent error), LeNet-5 (1998, about 60,000 parameters) on MNIST.
  - LeNet-based systems read a substantial fraction of US checks around 2000.
  - CNNs paused in the 2000s for lack of compute and data, then drove the 2012 deep learning breakthrough.
